    Why Building Trust Through Real People Stands The Test Of Time In SEO & AI Search via @sejournal, @lilyraynyc

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that when it comes to organic search marketing, a loophole is not a strategy.
    • Industry observers note that any SEO who has worked in the field for a while has inevitably lived through a seemingly endless loop of fads, hype cycles, and shortcuts aimed at tricking search engines (and now, AI systems).
    • Industry observers note that plenty of people in this industry have battle scars from these experiences, myself included.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that when it comes to organic search marketing, a loophole is not a strategy. Loopholes have expiration dates, and in many cases, the time spent chasing them would have been better spent on work that doesn’t backfire later on.

    Industry observers note that any SEO who has worked in the field for a while has inevitably lived through a seemingly endless loop of fads, hype cycles, and shortcuts aimed at tricking search engines (and now, AI systems). Exact-match domains, article directories, parasite SEO, guest posting at scale, PBNs, programmatic pages, and now the AI-generated listicles, scaled AI content, and “inauthentic mentions” of the GEO era. Most of these things work for a while… until they don’t. And once Google, Bing, and more recently the AI companies themselves crack down, the sites that leaned on these approaches often end up worse off than if they’d never tried them at all, sometimes spending years cleaning up while traffic, visibility, and leads stay suppressed.

    Industry observers note that plenty of people in this industry have battle scars from these experiences, myself included. My first real SEO wins came from buying links in 2010-2011, and Penguin erased them in a single morning in 2012. Six years later, the 2018 “Medic” enhancement hit a client of ours that had been using AI and automation to scale medical content (long before this was popular), and it was the hardest hit from an algorithm update that I had experienced firsthand since the Penguin update. I think these scars are the badge of honor that inevitably comes with experience in SEO: thinking you know better than Google, and learning the hard way that you almost always don’t.

    All of that stated, there is one investment that has held up through every one of those cycles, and it’s the same approach I’ve recommended for many years: investing in real humans and placing them at the center of your marketing strategy. As AI makes generic content nearly free to produce, I believe that real, identifiable experts are becoming the clearest antidote to scaled, machine-generated slop. This article covers why, what the evidence shows so far, and how brands can consider “human-centric marketing” as a bigger part of their strategies.

    The list of spam violations Google laid out back then has carried on, in some form, for more than 20 years, right into the AI search era. I put together this infographic showing how Google’s original spam policies map to popular GEO tactics we see today with AI search:.

    According to recent reports, automation in particular has been in the crosshairs for well over a decade. In August 2010, Google’s John Mueller told a site owner that publishing Google Translate output directly “could be seen as creating auto-generated content, which would be against our Webmaster Guidelines,” and recommended having a human correct it first. By 2012, Google had published a dedicated help page on automatically generated content. Its examples included text “translated by an automated tool without human review or curation,” Markov chains, automated synonymizing, scraped feeds, and “stitching or combining content from different web pages without adding sufficient value.”.

    For what it’s worth, I still see this exact issue affecting sites today – perhaps more than ever – including companies who come to me after experimenting with scaled AI translations that get little human review. It’s interesting that John’s 15+ year old answer still holds up, although to be fair, most site owners have never read Google’s guidelines (and nobody can be expected to know about a forum reply from 2010). That’s what their SEO experts are (supposedly) there to help them with.

    In a recent development, funny enough, that 2012 list reads a lot like the sales pitch for the same AI content tools that have recently captured the attention of C-level marketers everywhere, many of which work in ways that come very close to (if not directly violate) Google’s long-standing anti-spam policies. It’s not a huge surprise that so many of the sites featured in their case studies have since rapidly lost organic traffic.

    Google’s wording has evolved since then, but the thread running through it has stayed remarkably consistent. In February 2023, a few months after ChatGPT introduced, Google stated it has “many years of experience dealing with automation being used in an attempt to game search results.” Then in March 2024, Google launched the scaled content abuse spam policy, which applies whether content is made “through automation, human efforts, or some combination of human and automated processes.” Automated translation, synonymizing, and stitching are still on the list, 14 years later. Marketers are now using LLMs to experiment heavily with all three. The main difference now is that generative AI sits at the top of the list of examples.

    Across more than 20 years of guidelines, the common thread is fairly simple: content made for search engines at scale, with no human reviewing it, adding to it, or standing behind it, eventually becomes a liability.

    When Google started using the acronym “E-A-T” in 2014 (now called “E-E-A-T”), it finally gave us a framework that reveals how to even do SEO work without getting caught up in the loopholes. Since then, E-E-A-T has been misunderstood, misused, and treated as a checklist or a single ranking factor that works the same way for every site (it doesn’t). In 2021, I even wrote an article aimed specifically at debunking many of these misconceptions.

    All of that being said, I still to this day believe E-E-A-T is the best framework we have for approaching our SEO/GEO strategies in ways that won’t be penalized or devalued later, and it gives us plenty of meaningful work to do once we focus on the right things. There’s a reason E-E-A-T is mentioned 120 times in the current version of Google’s Search Quality Rater Guidelines, and why Bing uses similar language, focusing on “quality and credibility,” in its own guidelines.

    Industry observers note that this type of work is people-first, meaning actual humans with lived knowledge sit at the center of the approach. It’s much harder than loophole-focused SEO, because it needs buy-in, time, and resources from the experts at the firm, not just the SEO team operating behind the scenes. But the return is high, and it affects more channels than just organic. It tends to stand the test of time; it’s good for your users and your conversions; it appears to help with AI systems; and it’s unlikely to get you penalized (unless you apply a shortcut mindset to it, which isn’t really an E-E-A-T strategy at all). It’s also the opposite of what folks publicly say they hate about the impact SEO has had on Google’s results, from The Verge asking whether SEO experts ruined the internet to a 2024 study finding product review results increasingly full of SEO spam.

    In a recent development, I’ve been preaching these same ideas for years, and I probably sound like a broken record to anyone who has followed me for a while (my MozCon 2022 talk was all about how to focus on real expertise, with numerous examples of real experts representing the brands they worked for). I even named my holistic approach to SEO/GEO the E-E-A-T Method and made it the core philosophy of my fresh consultancy, Algorythmic, because that’s how deeply I believe in the efficacy of this approach.

    But this wasn’t always a big focus in how I approached SEO; it’s something I learned the hard way.

    That 2018 Medic client I referred to before had been scaling a fast-growing library of health articles with no visible credentials from experts, and no sign of a real human behind any of it. When the upgrade hit, Google’s Danny Sullivan pointed site owners back to the Search Quality Rater Guidelines (his tweet has since been deleted, but Marie Haynes wrote about his guidance at the time). So I spent months reading and re-reading Google’s guidelines. Being the nerd that I am, I even printed and laminated a copy and kept it on my desk (which I admitted on stage in 2019 at BrightonSEO). When I read it, the answer to our client’s challenge became obvious, and it was repeated throughout the guidelines: the site was heavily YMYL (Your Money or Your Life) and showed nowhere near enough E-A-T for the health topics it covered and the medical advice it provided.

    The client wasn’t convinced at first, as this required a dramatic overhaul of their approach – so much so that we decided to part ways while they tried to bring back the site’s performance using their own methods. But after almost two years without recovering, the client came back to work with our team again. We worked together on a renewed SEO strategy, and about six months later, we relaunched the entire site, rebuilt from top to bottom around E-A-T, with human experts at the center: real doctors, real medical reviewers, and their original insights. The site climbed back to its previous levels after the re-platforming was complete. From the day the update hit, the full recovery process took more than three years. (This long recovery timeline is why I always warn sites to avoid getting hit in the first place!).

    Sources indicate that back in January 2019, the night before my first-ever conference talk at SMX West (which was – surprise! – focused on E-A-T), I sat at the hotel bar studying Mark Traphagen’s work on author authority. He, along with Jennifer Slegg, had been documenting the history of “authorship” and “author authority” on Google over time. (Funny side note: I ended up meeting Mark in person for the first time at the conference breakfast the next morning, a few hours before I went on stage, which felt auspicious.) After my presentation, when an attendee asked what a small site should do if its writers aren’t well known, my answer was to “cultivate your authors’ profiles, even if it means starting from scratch,” which ruffled some feathers in a room filled with technical SEOs who didn’t all buy into the idea that Google could figure these things out. Yet nearly eight years of research and client results later, I’m even more convinced that it can.

    Sources indicate that A few months later, Google’s official guidance on core updates linked to my BrightonSEO deck on E-A-T as a recommended resource, along with work from a few other SEOs. This solidified for me that E-A-T was becoming a big priority for them. In 2020, I had the great privilege of digging into the patents that might explain how E-A-T works with the late, great Bill Slawski, whose knowledge of Google’s patents was unmatched. This exercise helped me understand a more technical explanation for how Google’s systems might recognize individual experts. The following year, I took the topic to the MozCon stage with a talk on how the E-A-T ecosystem has transformed organic search.

    Sources indicate that “Humanize your brand” and “keep a human in the loop” have become marketing clichés of their own, so I want to be specific. By “real humans,” I mean practitioners with genuine expertise or experience: the doctor who has treated the condition, the engineer who built the system, the plumber who owns a local plumbing business, or the patient who lived through the illness. They earn their audience naturally, and across platforms, by sharing insights that are honest, original, often opinionated, and based on real experience. You can usually tell them apart from someone who highlighted up to sell you something, and if a sale happens at all, it tends to follow from the trust they’ve built.

    Recent findings suggest that my approach, for SEO, AI search, and broader marketing, is to put these real people at the center of the strategy whenever possible. It’s also what I’ve employed with my own personal brand (more on that later).

    In a recent development, I think this is the strategy most likely to survive whatever comes next, for a simple reason. Nearly every popular shortcut in the vicious cycle of SEO could be scaled. A real expert’s reputation can’t. It takes years of showing up, being right (and sometimes wrong, and open to admitting that) in public, and having other people vouch for you without needing to rely on inauthentic mentions or listicles calling yourself the best expert. As AI makes everything else cheaper to produce, I’d expect the value of that kind of earned reputation to keep climbing.

    In April 2024, on the Authority Hacker podcast, I summed it up with one of the sentences I’ve stated most often in my career:.

    “I’ve been talking about this for years: People like following people.”.

    It has been revealed that sidenote: Don’t mind the ghost opening the door behind me. That was my dog Marcy, who can never decide where she wants to lie down when I’m doing podcasts.

    It has been revealed that it’s no secret that folks on social platforms engage with other people far more than with brands. On LinkedIn, personal profiles outperform company pages by roughly 2x to 8x on impressions, depending on whose data you believe.

    Here’s what real people bring to the table that AI can’t:.

    Across platforms, signs of a real human may be the clearest way to separate spam and automated content from the content that provides the most value.

    In a recent development, A real human expert leaves evidence everywhere, and that footprint is easily detectable: photos from the conference they spoke at, video of the talk, a personal website (even a slightly neglected one), podcast interviews, years of social posts and replies, or journalists quoting them by name. I believe Google has systems in place to at least identify these signals, and likely reward them, from Knowledge Panels to the new Search profiles. The leaked Google documentation from May 2024 points in the same direction: it showed that Google stores the author of a document, and has an attribute called isAuthor that marks whether an entity mentioned on a page is also the author of that page.

    The typical fake author, on the other hand, has a stock-looking AI-generated headshot, a two-sentence bio (if any), and no other evidence of their real existence anywhere on the web. This approach isn’t limited to small sites, either: in 2023, Sports Illustrated was found publishing product reviews under authors who didn’t appear to exist, including one whose headshot was for sale on a site that sells AI-generated portraits. In that same year, fake authors were one of the most common patterns I found among sites hit by the Helpful Content Update, and in October 2026, Google added this exact tactic to its helpful content documentation: “Fabricating creator profiles (such as by using AI-generated headshots, made-up names, or false credentials to make content appear as if it was written by human experts) is a form of deception.”.

    Sources indicate that I predict that this trail of being a “real human” will matter even more as the web fills up with homogeneous vibe-coded sites. Anyone can now spin up a polished website in an afternoon, complete with a logo, a hundred blog posts, and a team page full of friendly AI-generated headshots. If you’ve looked at many of these sites, you’ve probably noticed they all start to look the same: the same purple gradient, the same three feature cards with emoji icons, the same “Trusted by” logo strip.

    According to recent reports, when a convincing-looking brand costs next to nothing and takes little time to build, polish alone doesn’t tell anyone very much anymore. What’s left are the signals that still take years to build: a real person or real people with real histories, who other real people have chosen to follow, quote, and recommend.

    Industry observers note that since the 2018 Medic update, Google appears to have spent the past 8 years building systems that reward exactly that kind of trail. In 2019, I analyzed 64 sites that had clearly won or lost across the 2018 and 2019 core updates, checking each one for 30 on-page E-A-T signals and researching the credentials of the people writing their content. The winning sites were 258% more likely than the losing sites to use real experts on their content (with the usual caveat that this was a small sample, and correlation isn’t causation). Since then, Google has put many of those same observations into writing:.

    Real experts and real lived experiences appear to drive a substantial share of AI search citations, and you can see it in which sites get cited most. YouTube and Reddit are consistently the two most cited websites in Google’s AI Overviews, at 24.5% and 18.1% of citations among the top 50 cited domains in Ahrefs’ November 2026 analysis.

    In a recent development, other studies point to LinkedIn, too. In a Semrush study of 325,000 prompts earlier this year, LinkedIn was the second most cited domain in ChatGPT Search, Google AI Mode, and Perplexity, and 59% of the LinkedIn content cited in ChatGPT Search and AI Mode came from individual members rather than manufacturer pages.

    This doesn’t surprise me – I’ve seen my LinkedIn posts and Pulse articles show up in Google’s AI search results immediately after publishing, like this test I did with a LinkedIn Pulse article about Google Discover. It earned the top ranking in AI Overviews and an AI Mode citation within seven hours of publishing.

    In other words, a lot of the information AI search systems draw on to build responses comes from the places where real humans go to share what they actually know, like a creator on YouTube walking through how they fixed something or which product they like best, a Reddit thread full of firsthand experience, or a practitioner’s thoughtful LinkedIn post or Pulse article. Unfortunately, these same platforms are also being flooded with AI slop, and it’s not a secret.

    Sources indicate that youTube and Reddit have been fairly explicit about what they want, and it also points to authentic human experiences. In July 2025, YouTube renamed its “repetitious content” monetization rule to “inauthentic content,” covering AI-generated videos made from generic templates “without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective,” and CEO Neal Mohan’s 2026 letter called out “AI slop” by name. Reddit CEO Steve Huffman wrote in February that “if you can’t easily distinguish a real person’s thoughts or recommendations from a bot, that trust erodes,” and a month later Reddit started labeling automated accounts. On both platforms, the most reliable path to visibility appears to be the one this whole post is about: be a real, identifiable person – sharing authentic and honest experiences – whom other people choose to trust.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve seen firsthand what sharing publicly can do for a business. When I joined Amsive, I had never given an SEO talk on a stage or done anything public-facing in the industry. Since then, in almost nine years on the agency’s SEO team, I’ve published research on its blog under my own name, alongside podcast interviews, conference talks, webinars, and other marketing efforts on the agency’s behalf. That work has brought the agency links, traffic, and name recognition that keep growing long after each piece goes live. When I recently looked at the agency’s backlinks in Ahrefs, a few things stood out:.

    Industry observers note that I’m sharing this because of where those links point: every one of them goes to the manufacturer. One person (or a team of people) sharing what they know under their own names can grow a company’s authority in a way that brand content on its own rarely does. I’ve seen the same pattern at countless other brands that put trusted experts at the front of their marketing, and I try to employ this same approach in my client strategies.

    It has been revealed that of course, I’m not the only example of this, and others in the industry are seeing success with the same approach. For years, Wix had what the Ahrefs blog called “a bit of a bad reputation for SEO.” Plenty of SEOs would have steered clients away from it. Then Wix did something smart: it hired respected SEOs like Crystal Carter and Mordy Oberstein to represent the brand within the SEO community.

    Industry observers note that crystal joined in 2022, and since then she has spoken at many major search and marketing conferences, co-hosted Wix’s SERP’s Up podcast, and published her own research on the Wix site. Today, when SEO publications write about whether Wix is good for SEO, they often point to her by name. That same Ahrefs article credits her and Mordy with pushing for “more SEO features and better communication.” About 1 in 20 sites linking to Wix’s SEO Hub mention Crystal by name, the podcast shows up in “best SEO podcasts” roundups from Backlinko and Ahrefs, and her expert page is the most-linked expert profile on the hub.

    For a more famous example outside our industry, look at travel expert Rick Steves. He self-published his first travel guide in 1980, and he has spent about four months a year in Europe for decades, walking the routes himself and updating his guidebooks every year. That one person’s lived experience grew into a tech giant with more than 100 employees, a PBS series that has run since 2000, a thriving forum and online community, a public radio show, and a tour program that takes more than 30,000 travelers to Europe each year.

    Recent findings suggest that I wrote about his site on LinkedIn this summer, calling it the ultimate embodiment of E-E-A-T and the perfect example of an expert-led marketing approach. He tells you – from firsthand experience – what’s overrated, overpriced, or skippable, and because he makes money from books and tours, his content is free from affiliate influence. His honesty is the product. Google’s AI Overviews often cite his website, and his YouTube and TikTok pages too.

    Industry observers note that brands that can should start by identifying the real experts inside the company and investing in making them visible. In practice:.

    Sources indicate that two fair counterpoints, since this approach isn’t possible for every firm: Some industries have compliance teams that make personal posting genuinely hard. And people may leave the company and take their personal brands with them. My answer is to try to build several voices instead of relying on one (my friend and colleague Viola Eva recently wrote about how they do exactly this at her company, Flow Agency). Furthermore, remember that any links, mentions, and coverage earned while someone represented the company can remain as valuable assets for the company, even after they move on.

    In July 2023, I posted on LinkedIn that even if Google couldn’t tell AI content from human content, someone else could: “guess who else doesn’t like reading AI content? OWNERS.” The consumer research has since caught up. A Gartner survey this summer found that a majority of U.S. consumers say AI content has made them less trusting of brand messaging, and Emplifi’s 2026 research found that only 35% of Americans trust AI-generated content at all (not that everyone can necessarily tell the difference). I’d call it slop fatigue, and I think the platforms are finally responding to it (or at least trying to).

    Sources indicate that every tactic that has blown up in this industry, from the links I bought in 2011 to the listicles and paid mentions all over the internet in 2026, was scaled for the sole purpose of driving visibility in search. That’s also, almost exactly, the list of things consumers say they dislike most about SEO. Real experts and experienced contributors have the opposite effect: they contribute the things that make the internet human, and the most popular, widely cited platforms are working hard to preserve their humanness in an internet flooded with AI slop.

    There’s another reason this holds up: your reputation is ultimately decided by what other people say about you, not by what you say about yourself. One of the rater guideline passages I put on a slide back in 2019 reads: “When there is disagreement between what the website says about itself and what reputable independent sources say about the website, we’ll trust the independent sources.”.

    According to recent reports, AI search is carrying that torch forward, as LLMs are getting better and better at determining someone’s reputation based on what others say about the brand or the person. That appears to increasingly include spotting self-promotion. Gemini now highlights its reasoning steps, and in this example (h/t Gagan Ghotra), it directly evaluated whether “Best AI SEO agency” lists were self-promotional, with agencies ranking themselves highly, to judge how objective those rankings were. Being genuinely recommended by other people is the most sustainable way forward.

    Sources indicate that people like following people. That was true before Google, and it’ll still be true after whatever comes next. The brands that figure that out won’t need the next loophole.

    This post was originally published on Lily Ray NYC Substack.

    Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 18, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff noted “Goodbye SEO” on X, promoting Palmata, an AI-based tool for tracking how visible a manufacturer is in AI answers, while a Salesforce guide linked on Palmata’s page states SEO “is still the foundation.”.

    In a recent development, benioff wrote in his post that customers “aren’t searching anymore” but instead are asking Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and other AI assistants which brands they should purchase. The post further states, “No click. No referral. Nothing in your analytics,” and then pitches Palmata as a tool that monitors what AI assistants say about a business, offers recommendations on what changes need to be made, and simulates the effect of those changes prior to publication.

    Several SEO professionals countered Benioff’s claims in quote posts and replies.

    Recent findings suggest that salesforce’s guide to SEO and AEO (answer engine optimization) claims SEO “isn’t going away” and that “SEO is still the foundation.” Graham Hardt, whose byline lists him as SEO Senior Director, wrote it for newly introduced businesses, and Salesforce published it Sept. 11. Palmata’s product page links to the guide from its FAQ.

    Recent findings suggest that contentful introduced Palmata in June; it became a part of Salesforce when Salesforce’s acquisition of Contentful occurred on Sept. 1. The article announcing the launch of Palmata, written by Jason McGhee, head of product and engineering for Palmata, noted that SEO gave organizations “a practical framework for improving visibility” and added, “That work remains essential.”.

    Aleyda Solis, an SEO and AI search consultant who founded Orainti, wrote in a quote post that AI search “relies on many of the same fundamentals as SEO.” Her post continues, “AI search optimization goes beyond traditional SEO, but it certainly doesn’t replace it.”.

    Solis also wrote that measuring AI search visibility matters, “but monitoring what AI platforms say about your brand and actually improving your visibility, recommendations and business outcomes are very different things.”.

    Pedro Dias, a technical SEO product manager who used to work at Google, wrote that SEO “was never a topic that attracted the interest of decision makers.” His post adds, “SEO isn’t traffic. It never has been.”.

    Lily Ray, who founded Algorythmic, replied to Benioff, “This gold rush already happened and the market is already oversaturated.” Growth advisor Eli Schwartz wrote that “there’s yet another AEO tool in the mix.”.

    When Benioff’s post is read by a marketing executive, Salesforce’s own guide answers it, stating that SEO and AEO are “two visibility layers for the same audience.”.

    In terms of making the case for new businesses to include both SEO and AEO, this guide provides Salesforce’s reasoning for including SEO in your plans right alongside any AI visibility tool, such as Palmata.

    Recent findings suggest that according to Palmata’s FAQ section, Palmata is a standalone tool that is also built into Marketing Cloud by Salesforce. In weighing tools like Palmata, Salesforce’s guide says you should track “both sets of metrics.” This means tracking your organic traffic and rankings, but also tracking how many times you’ve been cited by AI.

    WordPress Random Redirects, Branded API Data & CDN Advice – SEO Pulse via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates include a WordPress default that you will need to decide on, newly introduced data from Search Console via the API, and the question of which party determines whether Googlebot, AI agents or Google’s own calls will be allowed through.
    • WordPress 7.2 will introduce a /random/ redirect (turned on by default), and Google has added branded data to the Search Console API.
    • WordPress version 7.2, which is scheduled for Dec.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates include a WordPress default that you will need to decide on, newly introduced data from Search Console via the API, and the question of which party determines whether Googlebot, AI agents or Google’s own calls will be allowed through.

    WordPress 7.2 will introduce a /random/ redirect (turned on by default), and Google has added branded data to the Search Console API. Google also published the referrer values its traffic sends and shared ways in which a CDN move could lead to blocking Googlebot. Ask Maps began contacting local businesses, and United Airlines included its AI agent rules within its terms.

    Here’s what matters for you and your work.

    WordPress version 7.2, which is scheduled for Dec. 8, contains a fresh feature called /random/, turned on by default, to send a visitor to a randomly selected published post. There is no option in the dashboard settings for this to be turned off.

    Key facts: According to the developer note, /random/ randomly selects posts and also custom post types as long as they are publicly queryable and have archives (unless the developer has registered them using 'randomable' => false) and excludes pages and attachments. The development code uses a 302 status code along with an X-Robots-Tag: noindex, follow HTTP header when it redirects the visitor but does not send that header on the post that the visitor arrives at. To turn the feature off, developers need the wp_enable_random_content_redirect filter, and the different spelling given in WordPress’s November developer news roundup isn’t found anywhere in the code.

    According to recent reports, testimonials for clients (and other custom post type entries) may never be accessed via navigation. When their post type is eligible, they can be reached through /random/, even if they have been set to noindex by an SEO plugin. Before you update, check which post types would meet WordPress’s eligibility criteria, and ask a developer to exclude those that should not show up.

    Read our full coverage: WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made.

    Teams using the Search Console API can now segment the data they pull into branded and non-branded searches without having to maintain a list of their brands as regular expressions (regex).

    Sources indicate that key facts: Three Performance report features were added to the Search Analytics API by Google on Nov. 16. The brandedClassification dimension works only with eligible properties, and according to the API reference, the data provided for this dimension starts on Feb. 21, 2026. Setting type to webMultimodal returns results from Google Lens, Circle to Search on Android and image uploads, and a fresh filterLists field allows you to filter by multiple countries or devices in a single request.

    For reports covering dates before Feb. 21, 2026, you’ll still need your own brand regex. Google’s announcement of the branded queries filter says “some queries may occasionally be misidentified,” so comparing the API split with the regex you already use can help you spot where they differ.

    Read our full coverage: Branded Query Data Is Now In The Google Search Console API.

    A google.com referrer lets you know in your analytics when Google sends a visitor, but it doesn’t show which source (Search, Discover or Google Images) was behind it, claims a new Search Central page.

    In a recent development, key facts: The page was listed Nov. 12 in Google’s documentation updates log. It says Google Search utilizes an origin referrer policy for its Search results; thus, the header will contain only the scheme and host, and not the search query. Referrers from Discover carry the values of the surface where Discover was viewed. Same-origin services such as Google Images send the same values as Search and Discover.

    Recent findings suggest that to distinguish Discover clicks from Search clicks, use Search Console’s Discover report rather than referrer data. If Google traffic appears as referral or direct in your analytics, Google’s page recommends checking whether custom channel rules, referral exclusions, or filters are reclassifying it.

    Read our full coverage: Google Explains How To Find Search Traffic In Analytics & Logs.

    A CDN can let Googlebot crawl your site faster before the CDN’s cache has filled, according to Google, and those requests then go to your origin server.

    In a recent development, key facts: On Nov. 11, Search Central posted Google’s explanation that a fast and reliable CDN may slowly increase a site’s crawl capacity limit, while a brand new CDN begins with an empty cache. The first visit to each URL is a cache miss, so the page has to come from your origin server, and crawlers visit far more of your site’s URLs than visitors do, with most visitors sticking to a small set of popular pages. When admins block all bots from their site using blanket bot protection, they can cause Googlebot to fail CAPTCHA challenges. If this stays in place, then the pages of the site begin to drop out of search results.

    Google’s advice for the move is to allow verified bots in the CDN and firewall settings, then pre-warm caches by fetching your most popular and frequently crawled URLs before switching traffic. Before enabling bot protection during the migration, be sure the verified-bot setting is turned on.

    Read our full coverage: Google Explains How To Avoid CDN Migration SEO Problems.

    Google’s Ask Maps has started calling some U.S. beauty, pet care, auto and home-repair businesses to identify available appointment times for customers.

    It has been revealed that key facts: On Nov. 16 a post from Google said that customers can use Ask Maps to find these appointments online and have it call local businesses, then see available time slots so the customer can decide where to book. The feature started rolling out on Android and iOS, with the ability to find appointments launching in the U.S. first. Google already makes automated calls to businesses for customers using Google Search and Maps, including booking appointments and confirming availability, and this process is covered in Google’s Business Profile help page.

    In Google’s demo, Ask Maps demonstrates four times for a gel manicure that it confirmed were available online.

    The setting Google documents for those automated calls is the “Bookings and inquiries from customers” option in Advanced settings in your verified Business Profile. However, Google’s Ask Maps post does not indicate if calls received via Ask Maps are subject to this setting. Check what you have set, and make sure whoever answers the phone knows these calls come from Google on behalf of a customer.

    Read our full coverage: Google Adds Appointment Finding & Business Calls To Ask Maps.

    Sources indicate that united Airlines’ website terms, updated Nov. 11, let search engines index its public pages but require written permission for any AI agent that searches, books or buys on its site or app.

    It has been revealed that key facts: The terms also bar using data from United’s site or app, such as fares and schedules, to “train, fine-tune, ground, evaluate, or otherwise develop” an AI model. As of Nov. 14, United’s robots.txt named no AI crawlers or agents. Separately, HUMAN Security’s October report found that Meta’s and OpenAI’s agents made about 90% of the agent requests on sites and apps it protects.

    Sources indicate that in HUMAN Security’s October data, Muse accounted for 59% of agent requests. Three OpenAI agents accounted for about 30% combined.

    Meta’s Muse publishes no user agent for a robots.txt rule to name, as Slobodan Manic wrote in October, so whether it gets in comes down to your terms and bot protection. Muse sent the most requests in HUMAN’s data, and bot rules can check the signatures some of its requests carry, whose key directory DataDome reported had moved to muse.ai by Nov. 9.

    Read our full coverage: United Lets Search Engines Index Its Site, Makes AI Agents Ask First and Meta & OpenAI Agents Made Nearly 90% Of Agent Requests In Bot Data.

    In a recent development, much of this week’s SEO work sits with teams outside of SEO. The next steps for this week include identifying who is responsible for the off switch for the /random/ redirect, as well as reporting on the branded split and the analytics rules for referrers. Google’s CDN advice should be reviewed by whoever runs the CDN and firewall, and the automated calls toggle is managed through the Business Profile. United’s rules related to agents are contained within a legal agreement. Before the next change, the first step is to determine who has responsibility for each of these in your own organization.

    Senior Forward Deployed Engineer at Clutch

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1447 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, clutch builds AI agents that work on behalf of credit unions.
    • Industry observers note that as a FDE you are one of the two engineers on an agent.
    • This is a senior engineering role, not a solutions or support role.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, clutch builds AI agents that work on behalf of credit unions. Emma, our collections agent, is live at five credit unions and handled 60,000+ member conversations in her first twelve weeks at one of them. Behind her is a growing portfolio: origination, fraud step-up, member (re)engagement and activation agents, all built on the same Agents Platform (TypeScript, NestJS, our own agent SDK, MCP, Temporal, promptfoo).

    Industry observers note that as a FDE you are one of the two engineers on an agent. You take it from "sold" to "live and performing" at a specific credit union: you sit in the discovery sessions, you build the integrations to their core banking and loan systems, you author and tune the agent's behavior, you run the live tests with their staff, and you stay with it through go-live and the first weeks of production. When something needs a person in the room, you are the one who flies.

    This is a senior engineering role, not a solutions or support role. You write production code in our monorepo every week: integrations, modules, and the agents themselves (prompts, tools, evals), together with the other engineers on the pod. The difference from a traditional engineer is that you are on site more often, you make judgment calls in front of the customer, and you own the outcome. What you learn in the field flows straight back into the product: defaults, playbooks, and the platform capabilities the next agent will need.

    You build; our AI Operations Managers deliver. The pod (pod lead plus engineers) designs and builds each agent in a high-touch way with the first customers. Once the agent is defined and live, AI Ops coordinates the implementations, configuration and ongoing success at the next credit unions. You hand them something that works and a playbook to run it.

    In a recent development, this role requires roughly 20% of travel on average, with one- to two-week stretches around kickoffs and go-lives. Based in the US, able to travel on short notice.

    You'll join the Agents team, a small, senior group operating as a startup inside Clutch: seven engineers, a dedicated AI product group, and AI sales specialists, working directly with some of the largest credit unions in the country. Every agent is staffed by a pair of engineers, one leaning toward the conversation and LLM side, one toward software and integrations, with a pod lead who owns the product day to day. There is no layer between you and the customer, and no layer between you and the platform team.

    The operating style is direct, written, and evidence-driven: BLUF updates, evals over opinions, business outcomes over ticket counts. The team is spread across Brazil, Argentina and the US and works async by default. Being on site is a tool we use at specific moments (kickoff, live testing, go-live), not a permanent posting.

    Ship your first production change to a live agent through the team's review process, and be able to explain how a member's call flows through the Agents Platform end to end.

    Learn one agent deeply: system prompt, tool contracts, orchestration triggers, compliance gates, and the implementation process from kickoff to go-live.

    Join at least one credit union implementation as the second engineer, including a live testing session with their staff.

    Map where the current implementation process loses time and where a default or a tool would have removed a round trip.

    Own the technical side of one credit union implementation end to end: core and LOS integration, agent configuration, testing, go-live, and the first weeks of production.

    Run the eval and tuning loop for your agent (golden transcripts, rubric judges, regression suite) and be trusted to change its behavior without a second engineer checking your work.

    Have completed at least two on-site visits and turned what you heard there into product decisions with your pod lead and PM.

    Contribute at least one reusable capability back to the Agents Platform that the next implementation will not have to rebuild.

    Have taken one net-newly introduced agent from sold to live at its first credit union, with data you can show the partner.

    Be the engineer credit union staff ask for by name when something in their deployment needs to change.

    Have written the implementation playbook for your agent well enough that the AI Ops team runs the second and third credit union without you.

    Be shaping what the next agents look like, because you have seen where the current ones break in the field.

    Sources indicate that 7+ years of software engineering in a fast-paced environment, preferably in SaaS and/or Fintech, with senior TypeScript and Node.js backend experience in a large codebase (NestJS, CQRS, schema-validated boundaries, dependency injection). We do not count years of AI experience; the field is too young for that to mean anything. We look at what you have shipped and how you reason about it.

    Integration and API engineering: secure service-to-service endpoints, third-party APIs, webhooks, and the patience to work with legacy banking systems that were not designed to be integrated.

    According to recent reports, security and auth judgment: OAuth and machine-to-machine auth, tenant-scoped access, secrets handling, no PII in logs. Our agents touch sensitive member data and operate under consumer-contact regulation.

    Industry observers note that customer presence: you can sit across from a VP of Collections, hear a request, and say "here is what I recommend and why", including when the answer is no. You are comfortable making calls in the room and owning them afterwards.

    Code-quality judgment under deadline pressure: you take on debt deliberately, name it, and pay it down, rather than gold-plating or leaving silent debt behind.

    Genuine appetite for LLM agents: eval discipline for non-deterministic systems, reading a system prompt like code, understanding that some decisions must never reach the model. Curiosity plus shipped work is enough; research depth is not required.

    Nice to have, explicitly not required: voice and telephony (LiveKit, Twilio), Temporal or event-driven orchestration, Python, core banking or LOS integration experience, credit union or banking domain knowledge.

    Remote Flexibility: Enjoy the freedom of remote work from anywhere, balancing life and career seamlessly.

    Unforgettable Off-Sites: Twice a year, bond with colleagues in exciting destinations, fostering teamwork and fresh ideas.

    Paid Time Off: Enjoy flexible PTO days yearly for relaxation and rejuvenation.

    Stock Options: Joining us means having a stake in our success, so you'll receive stock options as part of your compensation package.

    Home Office Setup: Create your ideal workspace with a dedicated budget for home office essentials.

    Work Trip Budget: Grow personally and professionally with a budget for work-related trips and co-working.

    Health Coverage: Prioritize your well-being with comprehensive health and dental insurance looks.

    Clutch is a revolutionary vertical SaaS company, proudly backed by Andreessen Horowitz (A16z), aimed at revolutionizing the way Credit Unions engage and change the lives of their members. As a champion of financial well-being, we address the urgent need for affordable lending solutions in an era where the average American grapples with over $155,000 in household debt. Unlike traditional financial institutions, Clutch develops software to turn Credit Unions into FinTech lenders and leverage their balance sheets to responsibly lend to over 130M Americans. Our mission extends beyond mere financial transactions; we strive to fundamentally enhance the way credit unions interact with their members. By integrating cutting-edge technologies and user-centric designs, we help credit unions provide seamless digital experiences that are on par with leading tech companies. This approach not only preserves but revitalizes the longstanding tradition of community and member-focused service inherent to credit unions.

    Clutch is an equal opportunity employer. All applicants will be considered for employment without attention to race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, veteran or disability status.

    Salary TransparencyUS Tier I (SF, NYC, LA, Seattle): $176,000 - $210,000US Tier II (All Other): $158,000 - $188,000Actual pay may vary based on qualifications, skills, experience, and location. Base salary does not include bonus, equity, or benefits, which are offered in addition as applicable.Applications will be accepted on an ongoing basis.

    According to recent reports, our organization participates in E-Verify. Click here to learn about E-Verify.A Note About AI at ClutchWe love AI. We use it often and encourage our team to creatively and effectively leverage AI tools in their work. If you join Clutch, we hope you'll bring the same enthusiasm for exploring how AI can amplify impact, productivity, and innovation.That remarked, during the interview process, we want to hear your thoughts. Please approach interviews without the use of AI tools—our goal is to get to know how you think, solve problems, and communicate. Once you're in the seat, bring on the prompts!

    Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that liveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing.
    • The Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit is the technical owner and architect of the systems that power our go-to-market engine.
    • Salesforce is our system of record for revenue, pipeline, and customer data.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that liveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    The Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit is the technical owner and architect of the systems that power our go-to-market engine. You'll decide how our GTM stack is designed, what we build versus buy, and where we invest next — and you'll be hands-on building it: Salesforce architecture, integrations, enrichment pipelines, and the agentic workflows that help Sales and Marketing move faster and smarter.

    Salesforce is our system of record for revenue, pipeline, and customer data. HubSpot is our marketing layer for campaigns and lead generation, and what it captures needs to flow cleanly and reliably into Salesforce. Around them sits a growing stack of enrichment, sales intelligence, billing, and data platform tools. You'll own the architecture that ties it all together: disciplined change management, observable pipelines, data models built for AI consumption, and agentic workflows that act on GTM signals at scale — designed to serve the business for years, not quarters.

    Industry observers note that this role sits at the intersection of GTM, Data, Finance, and Engineering. You'll work directly with senior leaders to shape the GTM systems roadmap, turn business strategy into technical aims, and guide decisions that span multiple teams. You'll also help grow the engineers around you, setting the technical standards and practices the team builds on.

    In a recent development, you understand the difference between owning a system and gatekeeping one. Sales lives in Salesforce. Marketing lives in HubSpot. Your job is to make sure both are governed well enough that others can work in them effectively, and powerful enough that the GTM team can do things they couldn't do before.

    You'll thrive as a Staff GTM Systems Engineer if you:.

    Are known as the go-to person for tough technical problems, and have good judgment about which ones matter most.

    Think in systems and long time horizons, and can make confident architectural decisions with incomplete information.

    Can clearly explain complex technical concepts and tradeoffs to engineers and executives alike.

    Believe systems should be managed with engineering discipline.

    Ship fast and reliably — your work holds up in production.

    Are a fast learner, frequently picking up upcoming languages and tools.

    Find real satisfaction in mentoring other engineers and helping them grow.

    Own the architecture of the GTM systems stack: define how Salesforce, HubSpot, enrichment, sales intelligence, billing, and the data platform fit together, and write the technical strategy that guides how it evolves.

    Lead build-vs-buy and procurement decisions: evaluate vendors, run proofs of concept, assess security and integration fit, and partner with Director of GTM Systems and Analytics, Finance, Legal, and IT on selection and renewals.

    Shape the GTM systems roadmap with senior leaders across Sales, Marketing, RevOps, Finance, and Engineering: align on requirements, sequence investments, make clear tradeoffs, and lead cross-functional initiatives to completion.

    Own Salesforce as the engineering system of record for revenue: data model, flows and automation, validation rules, field governance, and access control.

    Own HubSpot for campaigns and lead generation, along with the HubSpot-Salesforce sync — so leads, contacts, and engagement signals reach the revenue pipeline without drift or silent failures.

    Build and maintain integrations across the GTM stack, and partner with GTM Analytics Engineering on reliable data flows to the central data platform.

    Design and deploy agentic workflows that consume GTM data, surface actionable signals, and automate manual operations — and set the patterns and guardrails others build on.

    Establish observability and change management for critical GTM systems: alerts, dashboards, and runbooks; reviewed code changes, documented config, and rollback paths.

    Mentor engineers across experience levels and set the technical standards for the team.

    Partner with the Billing Systems Engineer to automate the CPQ-to-Billing handoff.

    Extensive engineering experience in GTM or business systems, including owning a GTM stack's architecture end to end — build-vs-buy calls, vendor evaluations, and systems designed for a multi-year horizon.

    Deep, hands-on Salesforce expertise — you understand the data model, have built complex flows and automation, and you think about it as an engineering system, not an admin tool. This is the primary bar.

    HubSpot experience in a marketing context, including the HubSpot-Salesforce sync and what breaks and why.

    Technical depth beyond the UI — you've built integrations with APIs, webhooks, and event streams, and you know when a native tool (a Flow, a Clay table, a HubSpot workflow) is the right answer versus when it's time to write code.

    Agentic workflow experience — you've designed and deployed AI agents that act on GTM data in production.

    Strong change management practices — you've shipped changes to live systems while protecting active deals and campaigns.

    Experience influencing senior stakeholders — translating business strategy into system requirements and roadmaps.

    A history of mentoring engineers, from early-career to senior.

    Salesforce CPQ: approvals, order forms, discounting rules, and the closed-won-to-billing path.

    SQL and data modeling fluency; familiarity with a warehouse-centric stack (BigQuery, Snowflake, dbt, reverse ETL).

    Experience with billing platforms (Stripe, Zuora, Maxio) and the handoffs between GTM systems and billing.

    Experience managing a GTM tooling budget or vendor portfolio.

    Experience as a technical lead on a GTM or business systems team.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    LiveKit is an equal opportunity employer and does not discriminate on the basis of any characteristic protected by applicable law. If you require a reasonable accommodation during the application or interview process, please contact recruiting@livekit.io.

    Latest Update: WTF is a unified media platform?

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Sources indicate that this article is a WTF explainer, in which we break down media and marketing’s most confusing terms.
    • Editor’s note: These technologies are ill-defined, please share feedback to “editorial@digiday.com” to talk more.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Sources indicate that this article is a WTF explainer, in which we break down media and marketing’s most confusing terms. More from the series →.

    Editor’s note: These technologies are ill-defined, please share feedback to “editorial@digiday.com” to talk more.

    Recent findings suggest that ad tech has never been short on acronyms. Its latest crop includes: unified advertising platforms (UAPs), unified media platforms (UMPs), and unified buying platforms (UBPs).

    This kind of language has added a fresh layer of confusion to the space, and ad executives across adland have been saying, “WTF…?” Digiday is here to help by trying to bring some clarity to the matter.

    A simple way to approach the question is to think of such terms — UAP, UBP and UMP — as overlapping labels for technology that promises to make advertising easier to buy, manage and optimize across an increasingly fragmented media landscape.

    Sources indicate that of course, AI is central to the pitch. Advocates of such technologies maintain that instead of separately operating campaigns across Google, Meta, Amazon and the open web, advertisers could potentially use one system to determine where money goes, then execute those decisions through the relevant platforms.

    Sources indicate that some providers propose bringing buying and selling infrastructure together. Others want to sit above existing systems and coordinate them. This is an vital distinction to keep in mind, as connective software is not the same as controlling how an advertiser spends its next dollar.

    At its simplest, a UMP coordinates planning, buying, optimization, and measurement across multiple media channels. Its remit could include programmatic display, CTV, retail media, search, social, and direct publisher relationships.

    According to most sources, the idea is not necessarily to replace every existing media trading infrastructure, i.e., demand-side and supply-side platforms, etc., but to make them work together more efficiently.

    Industry observers note that that is distinct from the traditional remit of a DSP, many of which have spent years expanding the inventory and formats available through their own buying interfaces. A unified platform, by contrast, promises to operate across buying environments that no single DSP controls.

    Industry observers note that jay Friedman, co-founder of CartographAI, told Digiday that the emerging proposition is about budget fluidity, not simply consolidating DSPs and SSPs. “We define a UMP as a platform that executes buys across all primary digital channels (search, social, programmatic, and direct). This may or may not include agents,” Friedman told Digiday. “Traditionally, this has been the domain of agency order management systems,” he said, noting how several new entrants are hoping to challenge these players.

    The terms overlap, but they differ in what they promise to unify. The chart below traces that range, from handling an individual transaction to coordinating campaigns across channels and deciding where budgets go.

    Industry observers note that keith Weisberg of Unplugged Collective told Digiday UBPs would initially come to market as a repackaging of existing tools. He mentioned the deeper shift would come when buyers could bring their data to the places ads run and delegate spending decisions to AI agents.

    “I’d treat that as a net-new product, not a DSP feature,” he remarked. “However, we’re all plugged into DSPs, and even if it’s a new product, it’ll roll out via our current commercial relationships, because that trust (and legal contracting) took years.”.

    Industry observers note that ana Milicevic, co-founder of Sparrow Advisers, described the labels as directional distinctions rather than settled product categories. She added, “It’s not all just a collection of black boxes. Then that’s a net latest layer in the stack.” The key distinction is whether a platform merely pushes buttons in existing interfaces or makes independent decisions about where budgets go.

    Sources indicate that ciarán O’Kane, general partner at First Party Capital, was more skeptical about novelty. In wording expressly cleared for attribution, he characterized UMPs and UBPs as “meta DSPs” that act as workflow layers on top of existing systems by plugging into APIs. He also remarked many emerging players in the space that use this terminology are revisiting approaches the industry has tried before.

    Media-buying teams have long struggled with the fragmentation of conducting ad campaigns using different buying interfaces, datasets, and measurement methods. AI can make the operational work of combining and interpreting those inputs less expensive, but it does not automatically create comparable performance data or independent buying authority.

    In a recent development, “The frustration is very, very old. What’s latest now is that AI is letting us operationally skip through some hurdles that were previously insurmountable,” Milicevic told Digiday. Tasks that once demanded a substantial analytics stack and specialist labor can increasingly be assisted by repeatable prompts and automated processes.

    The commercial question is whether cheaper orchestration creates an entirely fresh buyer or simply a more convenient way to operate existing platforms. For advertisers, that distinction determines whether the new technology saves money, reallocates money, or merely adds another vendor to pay.

    In a recent development, in an Oct. 8 blog post, titled “universal buying platform,” Apostrophe co-founders Brian O’Kelley and Anne Coghlan outlined a broader buying layer intended to connect intent, execution, and measurement across advertising environments, citing the recent launch of Amazon Ads Agent as an example of this trend.

    Their argument is a public proposal, not evidence that a single independent platform already performs every part of the workflow at scale — O’Kelley did not respond to Digiday’s request for comment by press time.

    Other companies are approaching the problem from different directions, with Olyzon — an entity that used the term “agentic orchestration platform” in its recent CTV launch material — serving as one example.

    Jules Minvielle, co-founder and CEO of Olyzon, told Digiday the tech giant does not own inventory and uses agents to coordinate buying through existing platforms, with advertiser-controlled approvals. “A DSP is one place where you can buy. Orchestration is all the work around the buy: building the initiative, deciding where each dollar goes, activating across every platform, watching delivery, measuring, and feeding what worked into the next plan,” he wrote in an emailed statement, adding that uneven API access and inconsistent measurement remain substantial obstacles.

    In a recent development, ravi Patel, co-founder and CEO of SWYM.ai, drew a distinction between a common interface and control over the budget. “It can manage the ‘what’ and the ‘how much.’ It can’t manage the ‘which impression.’ That distinction is the whole story,” he explained, adding that campaign setup and pacing across platforms are already possible through APIs. However, impression-level optimization within the major walled gardens remains in their own systems.

    Recent findings suggest that lucas Cridland, CEO of Basin Media, questioned whether agents are changing the underlying buying process. “At the moment, many environments are agentically operating in the same supply chain flow. They’re just doing it with agents buying; they’re not radically changing the way the process works. And that’s where the real edge exists.”.

    It has been revealed that not necessarily. Many of the upcoming propositions depend on DSPs continuing to execute transactions, access inventory, and optimize within their own environments. The change may be who decides which platform gets the advertiser’s budget in the first place.

    Milicevic maintained that “value always accrues to whoever is closest to the decision or outright owns the decision.”.

    Ergo, if DSPs cannot move upstream into genuine cross-channel decision-making, they risk becoming “dumb pipes,” i.e., a commoditized, essential infrastructure whose underlying value is less visible to buyers.

    Recent findings suggest that incumbent DSPs, however, have established advertiser relationships, bidding technology, data integrations and scale. They could develop their own orchestration capabilities. A upcoming intermediary would need to show that its independence produces better decisions, rather than simply adding another fee, according to several sources consulted for this piece.

    According to recent reports, agencies already coordinate campaigns across channels, negotiate buying arrangements and manage the systems needed to execute them. Friedman, a former long-time agency-lead, argued that unified platforms could challenge agency order-management systems while bringing neglected channels, including creator-led media, into a common workflow.

    Such a scenario would not eliminate strategic planning, creative development, or oversight, but it could change how much manual campaign administration agencies perform, where they develop proprietary expertise, and which services clients are willing to pay for, with AI at the center of many contractual renegotiations between advertisers and media agencies.

    Such a scenario would not eliminate strategic planning, creative development, or oversight, but it could change how much manual campaign administration agencies perform, where they develop proprietary expertise, and which services clients are willing to pay for, with AI at the center of many contractual renegotiations between advertisers and media agencies.

    The biggest obstacle may be the very platforms that independent systems are supposed to coordinate. Google, Meta, and Amazon control their own buying tools, data, and optimization systems. Access through an API does not necessarily provide the granular information or authority required to compare results and independently move budgets.

    Trust is also an glitch. A unified interface can display reports from multiple platforms without proving that the outcomes are comparable. Attribution windows, campaign objectives, and self-reported measurement differ across channels, meaning an independent buying layer needs a credible basis for deciding that one dollar is better spent in one environment than another.

    Friedman was skeptical that interoperability would resolve the underlying problems, and highlighted how Google and Meta are unlikely to make their systems interoperable. He further questioned whether agencies could build the context and routing infrastructure needed to translate employees’ instructions into accurate buying decisions, even if every platform supported the Model Context Protocol. “Interoperability won’t solve anything,” he told Digiday.

    In a recent development, greg MacDonald, founder of Chelsea Strategies, mentioned addressing media buying’s growing complexity could reduce spending on its mechanics and, over time, potentially improve advertiser outcomes. However, he remained cautious about how far unified platforms could go. “I’m skeptical that the walled gardens will give buyers more control than they have today,” he told Digiday, pointing to persistent difficulties with frequency capping across programmatic formats, let alone disconnected marketplaces.

    Industry observers note that “But you don’t have to solve every problem, and certainly not on day one to be useful,” MacDonald added. He compared the opportunity with programmatic guaranteed buying, which made the insertion-order process more efficient without fundamentally changing direct media buying.

    Meanwhile, Milicevic remarked the more plausible near-term customer may be a multichannel advertiser between the largest global brands and small businesses that largely rely on a single platform. She also stressed the need for independent validation of results, rather than taking each platform’s own reporting at face value.

    AI agents could help automate campaign setup, inventory discovery, negotiation, execution, and reporting. That makes agentic advertising relevant to the unified-platform debate, but not synonymous with it: automating tasks is different from making accountable, cross-channel budget decisions.

    It has been revealed that unplugged Collective maps seven ways AI could change advertising (see graphic below). Per Weisberg, two are central to the unified buying debate: how agents decide where to spend and how they carry out those decisions across platforms.

    Industry initiatives such as AdCP and IAB Tech Lab’s agentic work aim to establish ways for systems to communicate and execute workflows. Technical standards could reduce integration costs, but they cannot by themselves force walled gardens to disclose comparable data or surrender commercial control.

    Seasoned industry observers have seen enough buzz phrases come and go to feel confident enough to make tongue-in-cheek observations when a upcoming acronym becomes de rigueur among the industry’s chattering classes.

    “I saw ‘UMP’ and I thought: ad network,” quipped Terence Kawaja, CEO, LUMA Partners, a prominent investment bank in the space, speaking on stage at this year’s Prebid Summit – channeling the industry adage, “everything is an ad network.”.

    Meanwhile, one prominent industry source, who requested anonymity to preserve industry relationships, dismissed the latest acronyms as another serving of “word salad.” However, the barbs, playful or otherwise, raise a palpable industry debate: As AI makes it cheaper to run campaigns across platforms, who gets to decide where the money goes?

    Industry observers note that the clearest test is whether advertisers entrust meaningful cross-channel allocation to an independent system — and can demonstrate that the decisions improve outcomes. Smaller-scale automation and campaign management do not, on their own, prove that a new market category has emerged.

    Industry observers note that milicevic identified three indicators: real advertiser budgets moving under independent allocation, credible measurement outside any single walled garden, and changes in how marketing organizations structure teams. “If it’s truly structural, it’ll show up in the PNL, and if it’s slideware and fluff, then that’ll make its way into award entries and kind of the PR circuit,” she said.

    For now, the most useful distinction is between controlling the infrastructure through which ads are purchased and controlling the decision about where the money goes. The latter is the more ambitious promise. Whether anyone can deliver it independently, at scale, and at a cost advertisers will accept remains unresolved.

    Brands booking creators to make their ads are pushing up $116B global influencer market

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Brand spending on creator marketing is set to grow twice as fast as spending on advertising as a whole over the next five years, according to advertising research firm Madison & Wall.
    • The consultancy estimated that creator spending will rise 12% each year until 2030, versus a 6% increase in ad spending each year between 2025 and 2030.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Brand spending on creator marketing is set to grow twice as fast as spending on advertising as a whole over the next five years, according to advertising research firm Madison & Wall.

    The consultancy estimated that creator spending will rise 12% each year until 2030, versus a 6% increase in ad spending each year between 2025 and 2030. In 2026, the researcher estimates that marketers will spend $116 billion on creator activity.

    Driving that growth is ad spend intended to boost or promote creator content to a larger audience — which accounted for 44%, or $52 billion, of global creator marketing spending in 2026 — and brands paying creators to produce advertising assets for use in CTV, display and paid social contexts.

    The latter accounted for 12% of global creator spending in 2026, but will rise 16% each year until the end of the decade, making it the fastest-growing segment of the creator economy. Traditional sponsored posts or ambassador relationships accounted for 28% of creator spending.

    Brands attempting to reach large audiences on social platforms have begun to look to creators not just as a distribution point, but as a source of creative production that can meet the need for a diverse set of creative assets at a lower price point than traditional agency methods.

    Unilever CEO Fernando Fernandez, for example, recently mentioned that the CPG giant’s social content had to be constantly refreshed to prevent it from going stale. “The lifespan of a video today is four days,” he said during the firm’s recent Capital Markets Day. “Content has to be renovated because after four days you don’t have diminishing levels of return, you have negative marginal return.”.

    Industry observers note that “The reason we see brands engaging with this is just because it’s cheaper,” said Luke Stillman, managing director at Madison & Wall. “Everybody is trying to squeeze down all those non-working expenses as much as possible.”.

    According to recent reports, as creator rosters get larger — Unilever now works with around 500,000 — the need to manage such programs has driven spending on specialist agencies, platforms and talent representation. Spending on creator intermediaries (fees for specialist agencies, platforms, or talent representation) accounted for 8% of global creator spending.

    Sources indicate that stillman said he expected to see spending on that slice grow further in coming years. “Identifying the right creators, contracting with all those creators, managing non-delivery and legal issues and payment issues are really complex, and so there’s plenty of space for ancillary services there,” he said.

    It has been revealed that “We’re seeing an increase on budgets year-on-year from our clients,” mentioned Andy Ryan, co-founder at social and influencer agency Komodo. Ryan estimated client spending on creator marketing had increased 20%-30% in 2026.

    Olivia Wedderburn, head of influence at Born Social, saw an even bigger jump, estimating that client spending on creator activity had risen 50% compared with last year. “I would anticipate that will only continue to grow quite heavily,” she said.

    Sources indicate that the U.S. market accounted for 43% of creator spending last year, per Madison & Wall estimates, while the U.K. and Germany are the next-largest, at 5% and 4% respectively. The U.S. will see spending grow 15% this year. India was the fastest growing market, at 20%.

    Madison & Wall’s estimate for asset-led spending covered several related practices: whitelisting, fees for user-generated content, content licensing, and fees for producing creative assets.

    However brands are commissioning it, creator-led production is on the rise. “More of our brand partners are bringing creators in as the production engine for their paid media, not just their organic social,” noted Nicholas Spiro, chief commercial officer at Viral Nation.

    While cost is a major factor, as Stillman noted, agency marketers also believe creator-made work can engage audiences more effectively than an ad made for the same environment by a creative director.

    Sources indicate that “Creator-made assets simply connect best with potential customers on a human level,” mentioned Spiro. “They tend to drive performance better than traditional brand creative, and they can be more measurable for certain objectives than organic creator-only content.”.

    While creator marketing was once dominated by apparel and beauty brands, healthcare, automotive and finance advertisers now spend on creator activity too.

    “Where some sectors like fashion and beauty have been on this for a number of years, and therefore they’re already doing a fantastic job at it… some sectors [were] behind and they’re catching up and are now throwing more at it,” remarked Ryan.

    In a recent development, “An ad can make a claim. A parent can prove it,” remarked Carmen Graham, CMO at Genexa, a youth-targeted healthcare brand.

    “Parent creators can also do what we can’t: show the product in real use, in their home. The messier and less art-directed the medicine cabinet, the more we see ourselves and our customer in the content,” she stated.

    “Our bet is that this commitment to being parent-first will drive the trust this category requires — especially if you’re switching to a new product to support you in the most dire moments of parenthood.”.

    After 45 years of negotiating, the chairman of Publicis Media Exchange (PMX) U.S., is stepping down from a full-time role this year, although he looks to continue to consult with the holdco.

    Mediaplus and Publicis clients, including Banco Santander, have paused TikTok spending in wake of investigations into abuse images circulating on the video platform.

    A latest crop of companies promise to coordinate advertising budgets across platforms, but can they control buying decisions, or merely add another interface to the existing system?
